+// Plain-English definitions for the parser jargon the docs use, surfaced as
+// hover tooltips by <Term>. Keyed by a short slug; the visible text is the
+// component's slot, so the same term can read naturally in different sentences.
+export const glossary: Record<string, string> = {
+  recognizer:
+    "A parser that only answers yes/no — does the input fit the grammar? — without building a value or a tree.",
+  nonterminal:
+    "A named grammar rule (mixed-case in Gramaire), defined by its productions. Contrast a terminal.",
+  terminal:
+    "A literal piece of input — a quoted spelling like '+', or a token class like NUMBER.",
+  "token-class":
+    "An ALL-CAPS lexer rule (e.g. NUMBER : /[0-9]+/) that matches a family of input text, not one fixed spelling.",
+  "shift-reduce":
+    "A conflict where the parser cannot tell whether to read another token (shift) or apply a completed rule (reduce).",
+  "lalr-artifact":
+    "A conflict that LALR(1)'s merged states invent but canonical LR(1) or IELR(1) resolve — fixable by a stronger table method, no grammar change.",
+  lr1: "Left-to-right input, rightmost derivation, one token of lookahead — the parser class Gramaire targets.",
+  cst: "Concrete syntax tree: every token and rule the parser matched, brackets and operators included.",
+  ast: "Abstract syntax tree: the trimmed tree your actions build, keeping only what downstream code needs.",
+  "epsilon-free":
+    "A grammar with no empty (nullable) productions. Gramaire's desugaring keeps the generated core epsilon-free.",
+};

+---
+title: Overview
+description: Overview of the Gramaire project and documentation hub.
+---
+
+Gramaire places grammar, documentation, and generated artifacts in one Markdown
+document. The [fmt output contract](../../../../docs/fmt-output-contract.md) and
+the [IR schema](../specs/ir-schema/) make the grammar both human-readable and
+machine-checked. The real implementation is a Scala core, cross-compiled to the
+JVM (the `gramaire` CLI) and to Scala.js — the same code either target runs, so
+a verdict from one matches the other.
+
+## Where to go next
+
+- **New to Gramaire?** Start with the [tutorial](../../tutorials/intro/) — it
+  builds a small calculator grammar from scratch.
+- **Want the formal rules?** See the [language specification](../specs/grammar-format/).
+- **Looking for a schema or contract artifact?** See the [schema overview](../specs/schema-overview/).

+---
+title: Language Specification
+description: The formal Gramaire grammar format — document envelope, lexical rules, newline normalization, desugaring, and the IR/CST contracts.
+---
+
+import { Aside } from "@astrojs/starlight/components";
+
+This is the formal definition of the Gramaire grammar language (v0.1): the
+document envelope, the `lr` lexical grammar, the newline rule, the desugaring
+that compiles surface sugar to the epsilon-free core, and the contracts the
+compiler emits. Keywords MUST / SHOULD / MAY per RFC 2119.
+
+<Aside>
+  The canonical on-disk layout that `gramaire fmt` produces is specified
+  separately in the [fmt output
+  contract](../../../../../docs/fmt-output-contract.md). This page specifies the
+  _language_; that one specifies its _formatting_.
+</Aside>
+
+## 1. Document envelope
+
+A Gramaire grammar is hosted in a GitHub-Flavored Markdown document. The compiler
+ignores prose, list markers, and images; it extracts the grammar by scanning ATX
+headings and fenced code blocks whose info string begins with `gramaire`.
+
+- **Grammar name.** The single `# H1`. There MUST be exactly one.
+- **Nonterminal rules.** Every non-reserved `## H2` names a nonterminal; the
+  `lr` block beneath it holds that rule's productions.
+- **Reserved `## H2` sections.** `General settings` (a `gramaire settings` block
+  of document-level directives — currently `%lang <host>`, which declares the
+  language of inline `{% … %}` actions), `Precedence` (an `lr precedence` block),
+  `Error messages` (an `lr errors` block), and `Generated tables` (the emitted
+  FIRST/FOLLOW table). They appear in that order when present.
+- **Presentational headings.** `###` and deeper headings carry no structural
+  meaning; they are free grouping the analyzer skips. Only the H1 and H2 layers
+  are structural.
+- **One grammar per file.** A file defines exactly one start symbol and one
+  nonterminal namespace. Reuse across files is a future cross-file `import`,
+  never in-file sub-grammars or multiple H1s.
+
+## 2. Lexical grammar of an `lr` block
+
+Inside an `lr` productions block the lexer emits these token classes:
+
+| Token                     | Form                     | Meaning                                              |
+| ------------------------- | ------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------- |
+| `IDENT`                   | `[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*` | a nonterminal (mixed-case) or token class (ALL-CAPS) |
+| `TERM_LIT`                | `` `…` ``                | a backtick-delimited literal terminal                |
+| `:` / `\|`                | `:` / `\|`               | rule-head colon / alternative separator              |
+| `ACTION`                  | `{% … %}`                | a semantic action; body kept verbatim                |
+| `LABEL`                   | `# Name`                 | an alternative label (visitor / accessor name)       |
+| `ATTR`                    | `#[name]`                | a rule attribute (e.g. `#[inline]`)                  |
+| `PLUS` `STAR` `QUESTION`  | `+` `*` `?`              | repetition / optional postfixes                      |
+| `LANGLE` `RANGLE` `COMMA` | `<` `>` `,`              | macro-call punctuation                               |
+| `NL`                      | one or more line breaks  | structural newline (see §3)                          |
+
+A name is a **nonterminal** exactly when it appears as some rule's left-hand
+side; any other mixed-case name referenced but never defined is a build error
+(not a silent terminal). An ALL-CAPS name is always a token class. Input
+tokenization itself is per-language: the `lr` lexer reads the grammar; a separate
+lexer turns _input_ strings into tokens whose `terminal` names match the
+grammar's terminals.
+
+## 3. Newline normalization (Option A)
+
+A line break **inside an alternative is insignificant** — `|` is the only
+alternative separator, so a long alternative may wrap across physical lines. Only
+two newlines are structural, and a normalization pass keeps exactly those before
+the parser runs:
+
+- the **head** `NL` inside `IDENT NL :` (or `ATTR IDENT NL :`), which is what
+  distinguishes a rule head from a same-line `name:Sym` field (`IDENT : Sym`);
+  and
+- the **boundary** `NL` immediately before the next head.
+
+Every other newline — between two symbols, before a `|`, before a label or
+action, at a block edge — is dropped. The lookahead that classifies a newline
+happens once, in this pass, so the grammar stays LR(1) on one token of lookahead
+with no `;` terminators.
+
+<Aside type="caution">
+  A consequence: a `name:Sym` field MUST stay on one line. Splitting it across a
+  break reads the name as a rule head.
+</Aside>
+
+## 4. Desugaring to the epsilon-free core
+
+Before building tables, the surface grammar is lowered to a pure, epsilon-free
+context-free grammar. The core automaton never sees a nullable rule, which keeps
+table construction free of nullable bookkeeping.
+
+### 4.1 Repetition — `X+`, `X*`
+
+`X+` (one-or-more) lowers to a fresh left-recursive list nonterminal whose action
+accumulates an `Array`:
+
+```text
+X_plus
+  : X
+  | X_plus X
+```
+
+`X*` (zero-or-more) reuses that list but enumerates **present / absent** at the
+use site, so the empty case is a real production rather than an epsilon — the
+core stays epsilon-free.
+
+### 4.2 Optional — `X?`
+
+`X?` desugars by **use-site enumeration with generated wrapper actions**. A rule
+`A : pre X? post {% f %}` becomes two epsilon-free productions:
+
+```text
+A : pre X post   -- wrapper applies f with (Just x)
+A : pre post      -- wrapper applies f with Nothing
+```
+
+The wrapper splices the original action verbatim, so it still receives one
+`Maybe` and arity is preserved. With _k_ optionals an alternative enumerates to
+2^k productions; an all-optional alternative (which would enumerate to an empty
+production) is a build error, never a silent epsilon.
+
+### 4.3 Macros — `Comma<X>`, `Sep<X, S>`
+
+`Comma<X>` and `Sep<X, S>` lower to a fresh one-or-more separated-list rule
+(separated by `,` or by the given symbol `S`). An unknown macro or wrong arity is
+a build error.
+
+### 4.4 Named fields — `name:X`
+
+A `name:X` prefix names that right-hand position. The name is carried onto the
+IR's `rhs[].field` and feeds CST accessors and generated visitors; it does not
+change the recognized language.
+
+Under the declared `%lang` (currently `javascript`), an action receives its
+children as a single **namedtuple** `c` — an object read by field (`c.left`) or
+destructured (`({ left, right }) => …`), with the field names taken from
+`rhs[].field`. A production `left:NUM '+' right:NUM {% (c) => c.left + c.right %}`
+binds `c.left`/`c.right` from the explicit field names.
+
+A position with **no** explicit `name:` is still auto-named by its symbol
+(`Expr` → `c.expr`, a token class lowercased) — but **only when that symbol occurs
+once** among the rule's nameable positions (nonterminals and token classes;
+literals are never named). A repeated symbol (`Expr '+' Expr`) or a name that
+would collide with an explicit field stays index-only, with no silent
+disambiguation. Auto-naming is a codegen convenience; it does not alter the IR.
+
+### 4.5 Inline folding — `#[inline]`
+
+`#[inline]` marks a single-production rule to be folded into every use site and
+then dropped — both a DRY tool and a way to hand-fit a grammar into LR(1). When
+the using alternative has an action, the inline rule's own action is threaded
+through a wrapper so values still flow.
+
+### 4.6 Labels — `# Name`
+
+A `# Name` label names an alternative. It surfaces in the IR as an optional
+`rules[].label` and drives per-alternative visitor method names and CST accessors.
+
+For a host-agnostic AST, **prefer labels over inline `{% … %}` actions** (ADR
+D37). A label like `# MulDiv` generates a typed `MulDiv(children)` method on the
+emitted `Visitor<T>` — exactly ANTLR's `visitMulDiv` pattern — that you implement
+in any target. Inline actions, by contrast, are host source: the `%lang`
+directive declares their language, so a grammar that carries them is tied to that
+host (e.g. `%lang javascript` bakes a self-contained `evaluate(cst)`). So:
+
+```gramaire
+expr
+  : expr '*' term   # MulDiv
+  | expr '+' term   # AddSub
+  | NUM             # Int
+```
+
+emits `interface Visitor<T> { MulDiv(c): T; AddSub(c): T; Int(c): T; … }` — you
+fill in the methods in your host language, no inline lambda required. Inline
+`{% … %}` stays available for one-liners where a visitor class is overkill.
+
+## 5. The IR contract — `gramaire-ir`
+
+The compiler emits the analyzed grammar and its parse tables as a versioned JSON
+document, the [IR schema](../ir-schema/). Every backend reads only this artifact —
+isolating target generators from Markdown processing and layout entirely.
+
+```json
+{
+  "irVersion": 0,
+  "grammar": {
+    "name": "Calc",
+    "start": "Expr",
+    "rules": [
+      {
+        "id": 0,
+        "lhs": 0,
+        "rhs": [
+          { "ref": "nt", "id": 0, "field": "left" },
+          { "ref": "t", "id": 2 },
+          { "ref": "nt", "id": 1, "field": "right" }
+        ],
+        "label": "Add",
+        "actions": {
+          "javascript": "(c) => ({ tag: \"Add\", left: c.left, right: c.right })"
+        }
+      }
+    ]
+  },
+  "tables": {
+    "algorithm": "canonical",
+    "stateCount": 42,
+    "action": [],
+    "goto": []
+  },
+  "conflicts": []
+}
+```
+
+`actions` maps a `%lang` profile name to that language's opaque, untrusted
+source text — see the full shape in
+[`spec/ir-schema.json`](../../../../../spec/ir-schema.json).
+
+## 6. The CST contract — `gramaire-cst`
+
+An action-free grammar still fully defines a **concrete syntax tree**: a `branch`
+per reduced production (tagged with its `rules[]` index) and a `token` leaf per
+consumed terminal, children in source order. This generic tree is the portable
+artifact any backend can emit and any host can walk; its shape is fixed by the
+[CST schema](../cst-schema/). The spanned tokenizer carries exact source ranges,
+so a tool can link a CST node back to both its production and its input slice —
+the substrate a hover-linking UI (planned) would use.
+
+## 7. Table construction and conflicts
+
+Tables build by canonical **LR(1)**, **LALR(1)** (canonical states merged by
+LR(0) core), or **IELR(1)** (LALR with the conflicting merges split apart).
+Canonical is the most powerful and serves as the differential oracle for the
+other two.
+
+A conflict is reported in grammar terms — naming the competing productions, not a
+state number — and classified by comparing the three methods: a conflict LALR(1)
+reports but canonical / IELR resolve is an **LALR artifact** (build with IELR);
+one that survives canonical LR(1) is **genuine** (the grammar is ambiguous or not
+LR(1)). For genuinely ambiguous grammars the GLR engine returns the full parse
+forest — every derivation of the input.

+ +## 1. The shape of a `.gram.md` file + +A grammar file is a canonical Markdown document with a fixed structure: + + + +1. **One `# H1`** — the grammar's name. + +2. **One `## H2` per nonterminal** — the heading names the rule; a `gramaire` + fenced block under it holds its productions. + +3. **Reserved `## H2` sections** — `General settings`, `Precedence`, `Error +messages`, and `Generated tables`, in that order, when present. + +4. **Everything else is prose** — paragraphs, images, and `###`+ headings are + free presentational grouping the compiler ignores. + + + +One file is exactly one grammar: one start symbol, one namespace. Productions +live in fenced blocks whose info string is `gramaire`; everything outside them is +documentation that travels with the grammar. + +## 2. Your first rule + +Create `calc.gram.md` and give it a title and a first nonterminal: + +````md +# Calc + +A small arithmetic grammar. + +## Expr + +An expression is a sum or difference of terms. + +```gramaire +Expr + : Expr '+' Term + | Expr '-' Term + | Term +``` +```` + +Reading the `gramaire` block: + +- `Expr` on its own line names the nonterminal; the `:` on the next line begins + its alternatives. +- `|` separates alternatives — and it is the **only** separator. A line break + inside an alternative is insignificant, so a long alternative may wrap freely. +- Quoted spellings like `'+'` (single or double quotes) are **literal + terminals** — the exact text to match. +- A **mixed-case** name (`Expr`, `Term`) is a nonterminal; an **ALL-CAPS** name + (`NUMBER`) is a lexer token class. A mixed-case name you never define is a + missing rule — Gramaire rejects it by name rather than treating it as a phantom + terminal. + +
+ A rule head is `Name` on its own line, then `:` on the next — the line break + is load-bearing. It is the one thing that distinguishes a head from a + `name:Sym` **field** (written `IDENT : Sym` with no break, see §4). So never + write a head inline as `Name : …`. +
+ +Add the remaining rules — `Term`, then `Factor` for numbers and parentheses: + +```gramaire +Term + : Term '*' Factor + | Term '/' Factor + | Factor + +Factor + : '(' Expr ')' + | NUMBER +``` + +`Factor` mentions the `NUMBER` token class but nothing has said what a `NUMBER` +_is_ yet. Declare token classes in a reserved `## Tokens` section, each an +ALL-CAPS name bound to a `/regex/`; mark throwaway classes (whitespace) `%skip`: + +````md +## Tokens + +```gramaire tokens +NUMBER : /[0-9]+/ +WS : /[ \t\r\n]+/ %skip +``` +```` + +That is the whole recognizer's vocabulary. Gramaire renders each rule as a +**railroad diagram** — the same SVGs `gramaire fmt` writes back into your +`.gram.md`, so the committed file documents itself. Here is the calculator's +shape, the stratification visible at a glance: + + + +We will run it in §5; first, two conveniences. + +## 3. Surface sugar + +Writing pure, left-recursive, epsilon-free productions by hand is wordy. +Gramaire gives you sugar that compiles down to that clean core automatically +(`Gramaire.Desugar`), so the table generator never sees a nullable rule. + + + + `X+` one-or-more, `X*` zero-or-more, `X?` optional. `X+` becomes a fresh + left-recursive list; `X*` and `X?` enumerate present/absent at the use site, + so the core stays epsilon-free. + + + `Comma` and `Sep` expand to one-or-more lists separated by `,` or by + any symbol `S` — e.g. `'{' Comma '}'`. + + + `left:Expr` names a right-hand position. The name rides onto the IR + (`rhs[].field`) and drives generated CST accessors and visitors — without + changing the recognized language. + + + `#[inline]` on a rule folds its single production into every use site, then + drops it — a DRY tool, and a way to hand-fit a grammar into LR(1). + + + +For example, a statement block is just: + +```gramaire +Block + : '{' Sep '}' +``` + +## 4. Precedence and conflicts + +A shift/reduce conflict is what a recursive, +ambiguous operator grammar produces. Declare operator precedence in a reserved +section to resolve it — earlier declarations bind more loosely: + +````md +## Precedence + +```gramaire precedence +%left '+' '-' +%left '*' '/' +``` +```` + +When a build _does_ conflict, Gramaire never tells you "conflict in state 7." It +names the competing rules — "shift `+` vs reduce `Expr -> Expr + Expr`" — and it +can tell you _what kind_ of conflict it is: + +- an **LALR artifact** — canonical LR(1) or + IELR(1) resolves it, so just build with a stronger method; +- **resolved by declaration** — your `%left`/`%right` lines already clear it, so + the grammar compiles as written; or +- a **genuine** conflict — the grammar really is ambiguous or not LR(1) _even + with_ the declared precedence, and needs a refactor, another precedence rule, + or the GLR engine. + +```sh +gramaire explain-conflict calc.gram.md +``` + +## 5. Run the recognizer + +That is a complete grammar — and as it stands it is a **recognizer**: it answers +exactly one question, _does this input fit?_ Check it with the CLI: + +```sh +gramaire check calc.gram.md +``` + +`check` validates the grammar's own structure — no conflicts, well-formed +fences, defined nonterminals. Testing arbitrary _input_ against the grammar +interactively (`12 + 3 * 4` → accepted, `12 +` → rejected) is exactly what the +planned Lab is for; until it ships, the same table-driven parser this grammar +compiles to is exercised by the test suite and by `gramaire conformance`, so a +verdict there is the same verdict the CLI would give a specific input. + +
+ Linters, validators, and syntax highlighters often need nothing more than + yes/no. If that is all you want, you are done. The rest of this tutorial is + **Part 2** — turning an accepted parse into a value. +
+ +## 6. From recognition to a value + +A recognizer throws its work away. To keep it — to build a number, or an AST — +attach a host-language **action** between `{%` and `%}`. Declare the action +language once, in a reserved `## General settings` section: + +````md +## General settings + +```gramaire settings +%lang javascript +``` +```` + +With `%lang javascript` declared, an action is a JS arrow function receiving one +argument — a **namedtuple** `c` — built from the alternative's right-hand +symbols: + +```gramaire +Expr + : Expr '+' Term {% (c) => ({ tag: "Add", left: c.expr, right: c.term }) %} + | Expr '-' Term {% (c) => ({ tag: "Sub", left: c.expr, right: c.term }) %} + | Term +``` + +A position with no explicit `name:` is auto-named by its symbol — `Expr` becomes +`c.expr`, a token class lowercases the same way — but **only when that symbol +occurs once** among the rule's nameable positions. `Expr '+' Term` has two +different symbols (`Expr`, `Term`), so both auto-name cleanly; a rule with two +`Expr`s on one alternative would need explicit `name:` fields instead, since a +repeated symbol can't auto-name without colliding. + +
+ The parser first builds a concrete syntax tree — every + token it matched, the `+` and the parentheses included. Your actions project + that onto the abstract syntax tree you actually want: + the `Add`/`Sub` actions above keep the two operands and drop the `+`/`-`; `'(' + Expr ')'` returns the inner `Expr` and drops both brackets. Same recognized + language, smaller tree. +
+ +If you'd rather name a position explicitly than rely on auto-naming — useful +when a symbol repeats, or just for readability — a `name:` field does it: + +```gramaire +Expr + : left:Expr '+' right:Term {% (c) => ({ tag: "Add", left: c.left, right: c.right }) %} +``` + +The field name becomes the `c` key regardless of the symbol's own name, so +`c.left`/`c.right` read in terms of your grammar, not its shape. + +
+ Actions are carried verbatim into the [IR](../../specs/ir-schema/); each + backend reads only the IR. The TypeScript backend, for instance, emits a + runnable parser and a typed Visitor over the CST without ever seeing your + Markdown. +
+ +## 7. Emit a parser + +At the CLI, check the file and emit artifacts from the same grammar: + +```sh +# verify the file (structure, formatting, no conflicts) +gramaire fmt calc.gram.md + +# emit artifacts from the same grammar +gramaire emit --backend ebnf calc.gram.md # W3C-style EBNF +gramaire emit --backend ts calc.gram.md # a runnable TS parser + Visitor +gramaire emit --backend ir calc.gram.md # the gramaire-ir JSON +``` + +`gramaire fmt` also writes the railroad diagrams and the FIRST/FOLLOW table back +into the document, so the file you commit renders as complete documentation. + +## Where next + + + + + +
